subject: treasureHoard
pitch:
Category: Prop group.
Subject: treasure hoard: coins, gems, chest, crown, goblets.
Style: League of Legends.
reasoning:
I need a root joint even though this is a props group without articulated parts, so I'll set up a base joint to satisfy the builder's requirement. Going for a League of Legends-style treasure hoard look: painterly, saturated gold, glowing gems, teal/purple magic accents, stylized and chunky.

I'm planning out the scene composition: a rocky cave-floor base, an open treasure chest with a hinged half-cylinder lid, mounds of gold coins scattered with a crown on top, two goblets (one upright, one tipped), and clusters of glowing gems in various colors using octahedron and icosahedron shapes. I'm sticking to well-supported builder calls like part, lathe, extrude, sweep, rod, stick, and cards, plus SVG textures and paint, since I can't test the API directly and need to stay within reliable patterns. I'm also considering a few extra flourishes like a pearl necklace or small candle, while keeping the core prompt elements—coins, gems, chest, crown, goblets—as the focus.

I'm sizing the hoard at roughly 1.6m diameter and 0.9m tall with the chest around 0.8m wide, making sure everything sits flush on y=0 with a rock-disc base about 1m radius and 0.08m thick. I'm setting up the imports from the core SDK module and the glow and clockwork kits, double-checking which helper functions are actually exported before relying on them, and starting to define the root joint for the hierarchy.

Now I'm thinking through the joint structure—since props can attach without a bone and default to the root, I'm adding a separate hinge joint for the chest lid so I can animate it opening via a pose rotation, weighing whether to build the lid pre-rotated in model space versus posing it with an axis/degree rotation after construction.

I settle on the simpler approach: build the lid parts attached to the hinge joint while it's still in the closed orientation, then apply a negative rotation around X to swing it open and lean back, since parts rigidly follow their bone's pose. I'll build the lid's half-cylinder geometry first, then pose the joint, and add any loose contents like coins afterward so they stay attached to the root rather than the lid.

Still defining the arch outline...

Placing the lid hinge at the top-back of the chest body, with its outline extending forward in z, and treating body coordinates in model space so parts align correctly in the closed pose.

I'm figuring out the chest body dimensions and position near the base, deciding to keep everything axis-aligned rather than tilting the whole assembly for simplicity, then starting to assemble the wooden box geometry.

For the interior, I'm planning a solid box with a gold coin mound covering the top rim, avoiding the complexity of hollowing out the chest. I'll generate the coins as merged cylinder geometries scattered with random tilts across the mound surface, using BufferGeometryUtils to combine hundreds of low-poly coin shapes into one efficient mesh.

Grouping coins into gold, gilt, and silver color batches...

For a handful of hero coins I could add an actual emblem texture, using cylinder cap UV mapping so the design wraps naturally onto the circular faces while the sides show a thin strip of the same texture.

Now I'm designing a gem helper using a lathe-rotated profile with low segment count for flat faceted shading, sketching out the crown's cross-section points to get that cut-gem look.

Dropping to around 0.45 keeps the emissive glow bright while still letting diffuse lighting show facet variation, so I'll go with flat color plus 0.45 glow instead of per-facet painting. I'll build the gem with a lathe geometry (6-8 segments) rotated along a custom axis to tilt it, rather than using a stretched octahedron.

For placement, I'm scattering gems across coin piles and adding a glowing crystal cluster behind the chest using taller lathe profiles with sharper points, tinted teal and purple for a Hextech/Void aesthetic.

Now I'm designing a heroic crown — a lathed ring band with extruded spikes and ball tips, gold with blue gems, sized proportionally to a head (~0.19m diameter) but scaled up slightly for heroic presence, with band height around 0.06 and spike height around 0.1.

Computing crown point positions manually with trig instead of relying on the ring helper, placing eight kite-shaped spikes with orbs around the circle, each oriented outward with its tangent facing upward along the axis.

Checking the cross product confirms the thickness direction points radially outward, so I position each spike at the band's mid-radius with a slight bevel, then cap each tip with a small sphere orb for the gem detail.

For the gems, I'm placing cabochons at the band's embedded radius using a lathe geometry oriented so its axis points outward, and adding a larger central gem plus a velvet-red dome cap profile sitting inside between the crown points.

Now I'm sweeping a pair of crossing gilt arches over the crown's top using Catmull-Rom curves between opposing band points up to a peak, with a thin tube radius for the metal.

I'll cap it with a small orb and cross finial, and rather than tilting the crown for realism, I'll keep it sitting upright and build a helper function that applies rotation and position via quaternion transforms to place each local point correctly in world space.

I'm working out how to tilt the crown onto the mound, deciding to build mounds as overlapping lathe domes rather than a heightfield mesh, with coins scattered across their analytic surfaces using an array of pile definitions for position, radius, and height.

Each pile gets a parabolic height profile and a mottled gold paint, and coins are placed by sampling random points within each pile's disk while skipping points where a neighboring pile would bury them underneath.

Coin orientation comes from the surface normal (gradient of the height field) with added random tilt and spin, using an `aim(dir)` helper to build the quaternion rather than calling setFromUnitVectors directly, plus some coins get exaggerated tilts of 50-80° so a few appear to stick up or lean dramatically.

I'm merging each color group into a single buffer by transforming low-segment cylinder geometries into position before merging, then passing the combined mesh in as a single part attached to the root bone. I'm budgeting the triangle count carefully — roughly 550-700 coins at 8 radial segments each keeps the pile under the 60k triangle limit while still looking like a chunky, stylized hoard.

Now I'm working out how the coin mound on top of the chest should fit within the box's footprint, since the dome shape needs to stay constrained inside the chest's width and depth so it doesn't overhang into empty air — I'm sizing the radius down to roughly match half the chest's shorter dimension.

Actually I think a hollow chest is better: build it from five boxes (four walls plus a bottom), then fill the interior with a gold mound made from a scaled sphere, using the part scale option to flatten it into a low dome shape sitting inside the rim.

I'm generalizing this into a reusable dome-height formula for coin piles — treating each pile as a half-ellipsoid defined by position, radii, and height, so I can use scaled sphere geometry for every pile with the bottom half buried below the surface.

For coin tilt I'm computing surface normals numerically from the height function so coins rest naturally on slopes, and I'm checking which pile's height function is dominant at each point so coins only render on visible surfaces rather than overlapping inside other mounds.

For materials, I'm giving coins a mottled gold paint and the chest walls a wood grain texture built from boxes, though I need to think about how plank lines would wrap across box faces without looking repeated.

Writing wood paint function...

Still refining wood texture logic...

For the chest itself, I'm thinking LoL-style ornate design: dark wood with gold-trimmed corner brackets and bands, going for a dark purple-brown wood tone with teal accent details.

Now adding a hextech-glowing lock plate on the front body, gold corner studs via a merged-sphere helper, and a dark red velvet liner inside the lid.

Adding a thin red velvet plate beneath the lid's inner face to simulate lining, positioning it slightly offset from the base plane so it's visible rather than hidden inside the solid.

Now I'm working out the geometry for the lid's open pose at -110 degrees, calculating where the arched tip lands in y and z after rotation so I can check clearances against the chest body.

I'm also laying out the overall composition: an irregular rocky base disc about 1.2 units in radius, the chest centered toward the back, with a crystal cluster placed behind and to the left for visual balance, viewed from the front.

Now I'm placing coin piles around the scene—a big central front pile, smaller ones to the left and right, and additional piles near the chest to create overlapping depth. The crown sits on top of the center pile, slightly tilted forward, with goblets positioned on either side for symmetry.

I'm designing three distinct goblets: an upright gold one with gem accents on the left pile, a tipped-over gold goblet spilling a trail of coins on the right, and a smaller jewelled silver one standing on a small pile at the far right. I'm building each goblet as a single lathe profile defining the foot, stem, knob, and bowl shape.

I'm also considering a larger hero gem embedded in a chest lock as a focal point.
